entries.name: SGX-Listed Shares
entries.summary: Buying individual company shares listed on the Singapore Exchange, like banks, telcos or industrials, gives you a small ownership stake. You make money if the share price rises or the company pays dividends.
entries.analogy: Like buying a slice of a local bakery — you own a piece of the business and share in its profits or losses.
entries.minAmount: No fixed minimum — buy in board lots of 100 shares (or odd lots via some brokers), so cost depends on the share price
pros: Direct ownership recorded in your own name at CDP (if CDP-linked), not just on a broker's books
Highly liquid — trade any business day during market hours
Many SGX blue chips pay regular dividends alongside potential price growth
Wide range of familiar local sectors: banks, REITs, telcos, industrials
cons: Concentrated in one company — a single bad result can hit your capital hard
No guaranteed income; dividends can be cut in a downturn
Requires you to research individual companies, which takes time and knowledge
Smaller, less-traded counters can have wide bid-ask spreads
entries.bestFor: Beginners who want to learn stock-picking basics and are comfortable researching individual Singapore companies.
entries.eligibility: 18 years old and above, with a Singapore bank account and a CDP account (or a custodian brokerage account).

entries.name: US & Hong Kong-Listed Shares
entries.summary: Buying shares of companies listed on US exchanges or the Hong Kong Stock Exchange through a Singapore broker with international market access, giving exposure to global giants not available on SGX.
entries.analogy: Like ordering from an overseas online store — you get access to a much bigger range, but pay a currency-conversion 'shipping fee' along the way.
pros: Access to global sectors and companies not listed in Singapore, such as large technology names
US market has deep liquidity and evening trading hours in Singapore time
Diversifies your portfolio beyond the small Singapore market
Many brokers now offer fractional shares, lowering the entry cost
cons: Currency conversion (SGD to USD/HKD) adds an FX spread cost on every trade
Shares are usually held in the broker's name (custodian/nominee), not directly in your own name
US market hours fall late at night in Singapore
Foreign withholding tax may apply to dividends
entries.bestFor: Investors who want exposure to global companies and are comfortable with currency risk and custodian (rather than CDP) share holding.
entries.eligibility: 18 years old and above; a brokerage account with international market access (custodian or CDP-linked broker offering US/HK trading).

steps.detail: Pick a custodian broker (or CDP-linked broker with foreign market access) and complete online onboarding.

steps.title: Fund your account and convert currency
steps.detail: Move SGD into your account, then convert to USD or HKD, or fund directly in foreign currency if supported.

steps.title: Research the company
steps.detail: Overseas companies report under different accounting and disclosure standards from SGX-listed firms — read up before buying.

steps.title: Place your order during local market hours
steps.detail: US and HK markets have their own trading hours, which differ from SGX and from each other.

steps.title: Understand tax and dividend withholding differences
steps.detail: Foreign dividends may have withholding tax deducted before you receive them.

entries.name: Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs)
entries.summary: A basket of many stocks or bonds bundled into a single fund that trades on the exchange just like a share, giving instant diversification in one purchase. Most ETFs track an index, so fees are usually lower than actively managed funds.
entries.analogy: Like buying a fruit basket instead of picking one fruit at a time — you get a mix in a single purchase.
entries.minAmount: Price of 1 unit — many popular Singapore-listed ETFs trade under S$300 per unit
pros: Instant diversification across many companies or bonds in one trade
Generally lower ongoing fees than actively managed unit trusts
Trades throughout the day like a stock, so you can buy or sell anytime the market is open
Good building block for beginners who don't want to pick individual stocks
cons: Still moves with the market — an index ETF falls when the index falls
Some ETFs use derivatives (synthetic replication), which adds extra counterparty risk
Trading costs (brokerage plus spread) apply on every buy/sell, which adds up for small frequent trades
Not principal-guaranteed — you can still lose money
entries.bestFor: Beginners who want diversified market exposure without researching individual companies.
entries.eligibility: 18 years old and above with a CDP or brokerage account; some ETFs (classified as SIPs) may require a Customer Knowledge Assessment.

steps.detail: Search the ETF's ticker and buy through your broker just like a normal stock.

entries.name: Singapore REITs (S-REITs)
entries.summary: Real Estate Investment Trusts pool money from many investors to own income-producing properties like malls, offices or warehouses, and are required by regulation to distribute most of their taxable income to unitholders regularly.
entries.analogy: Like being a landlord for a shopping mall or office tower without ever having to fix a leaking pipe — a professional manager runs the property for you.
entries.minAmount: Price of 1 board lot (100 units) — varies by REIT
pros: Regular, often quarterly or half-yearly, cash distributions
Exposure to real estate without the large capital needed to buy property directly
Traded on SGX, so much more liquid than owning physical property
Professionally managed — no landlord duties for you
cons: Sensitive to interest rates — rising rates can pressure REIT prices and borrowing costs
Distributions are not guaranteed and can be cut if rental income or occupancy falls
Concentration risk if a REIT depends heavily on one property type or tenant
Some REITs use significant leverage (gearing), which adds risk
entries.bestFor: Beginners seeking regular income and property exposure without the capital and hassle of direct property ownership.
entries.eligibility: 18 years old and above with a CDP or brokerage account.

steps.title: Learn how REITs are structured
steps.detail: Understand the roles of the trustee, manager and sponsor, and how the distribution policy works.

steps.title: Check the REIT's property portfolio and gearing
steps.detail: Look at what kind of properties it owns and how much debt it carries.

steps.title: Review the distribution yield and history
steps.detail: Check how consistent past distributions have been, not just the latest headline yield.

steps.title: Place your buy order for a board lot
steps.detail: Buy 100 units (one board lot) or more through your broker, just like a stock.

entries.name: Unit Trusts / Mutual Funds
entries.summary: A professionally managed fund that pools your money with other investors to buy a diversified portfolio of stocks, bonds or other assets, priced once a day at its net asset value rather than traded continuously like a stock.
entries.analogy: Like joining a group tour where a professional guide (the fund manager) picks the itinerary for everyone's pooled money, and charges a fee for the service.
pros: Professional fund manager makes the buy/sell decisions for you
Diversification across many holdings in a single purchase
Wide choice of strategies — regional, sector, income-focused and more
Regular savings plans let you invest small fixed amounts monthly
cons: Sales charges and annual management fees reduce your net return, whether the fund gains or loses
Actively managed funds often underperform a comparable low-cost index ETF after fees
Priced only once a day, so you can't react to intraday price moves
Not principal-guaranteed — you can lose money
entries.bestFor: Beginners who prefer a professionally managed, diversified option and are comfortable paying for that management.
entries.eligibility: 18 years old and above; available via banks, fund platforms and financial advisers, or with CPF/SRS funds subject to approved fund lists.

entries.name: Singapore Savings Bonds (SSB)
entries.summary: A government-backed bond you can buy in small amounts and redeem any month without penalty, with interest that steps up the longer you hold it. It's designed as a safe, flexible way for individuals to save.
entries.analogy: Like a savings account from the government that pays a bit more the longer you leave your money untouched, and you can take it out anytime.
entries.minAmount: S$500 minimum, in multiples of S$500; maximum S$200,000 per individual (mas.gov.sg)
pros: Backed by the Singapore Government — among the safest investments available
Redeem in any month with no penalty and get back your full principal plus accrued interest
Low S$500 entry point, accessible to almost any beginner
Interest step-up rewards you for holding longer, without locking you in
cons: Returns are modest compared to stocks or REITs — pure capital preservation, no growth
A transaction fee is charged for every application, whether or not you're allotted
Popular issues can be oversubscribed, so you may not get your full applied amount
An individual holding cap limits how much you can park here
entries.bestFor: Beginners building an emergency fund or safe base, and anyone wanting a no-lock-in alternative to fixed deposits.
entries.eligibility: Individuals 18 years old and above, including non-residents; requires a CDP account (for cash) or an SRS account (for SRS funds).

entries.name: Singapore T-Bills (6-Month & 1-Year)
entries.summary: Short-term Singapore Government debt sold at a discount to face value — you get the full face value back at maturity, either 6 months or 1 year later. They're bought at auction and the return is locked in once you're allotted.
entries.analogy: Like buying a S$100 government IOU for S$98 today, and getting the full S$100 back in 6 months or a year — the S$2 gap is your return.
pros: Backed by the Singapore Government — extremely low default risk
Short 6-month or 1-year tenor gives flexibility to reinvest often
Can be bought with cash, SRS or CPFIS-OA funds
Yield is locked in at auction, so you know your return upfront if held to maturity
cons: Money is tied up until maturity — selling early on the secondary market may fetch a lower price
Yields move with each auction, so you can't predict future T-bill returns
No capital growth — return is limited to the fixed discount
Bidding too high a yield risks not being fully allotted
entries.bestFor: Beginners who want a short-term, safe place to park cash with a known return, rolling over every few months.
entries.eligibility: Individuals 18 years old and above with a CDP/bank account; also usable with SRS or CPFIS-OA funds.

entries.name: Singapore Government Securities (SGS) Bonds
entries.summary: Longer-dated Singapore Government bonds, from 2 to 50 years, that pay a fixed coupon every 6 months until maturity, when you get your principal back. They're the longer-term cousin of T-bills.
entries.analogy: Like lending money to the government for a set number of years in exchange for a fixed twice-yearly interest payment, with your original sum returned at the end.
pros: Backed by the Singapore Government — very low default risk
Fixed coupon gives predictable income over the bond's life
Range of tenors, from 2 to 50 years, to match different time horizons
Can be bought with cash, SRS or CPFIS funds
cons: Bond prices fall if interest rates rise, so selling before maturity may mean a loss
Longer tenors lock up your capital for a long time
Fixed coupon means no upside if rates or inflation later rise
Less flexible than SSB, which allows penalty-free monthly redemption
entries.bestFor: Investors wanting predictable, long-term income with very low credit risk, who plan to hold to maturity.
entries.eligibility: Individuals 18 years old and above; can use cash, SRS or CPFIS (OA/SA) funds depending on the purchase channel.

entries.name: Corporate & Retail Bonds
entries.summary: Bonds issued by companies rather than the government, paying a fixed or floating coupon. Some are listed on SGX in retail-friendly board lots as small as S$1,000; others are sold only to institutions with higher minimums.
entries.analogy: Like lending money directly to a company in exchange for regular interest payments — your risk depends on how likely that company is to repay you.
pros: Generally pays a higher coupon than government bonds, to compensate for extra risk
SGX-listed retail bonds can be bought in small lots through a normal brokerage account
Regular, predictable coupon income if the issuer stays solvent
Bond ETFs offer instant diversification across many issuers for a lower entry cost
cons: Credit risk — the company could default and you may lose part or all of your capital
Fewer retail-accessible corporate bonds are listed on SGX compared to stocks
Bond prices can fall if interest rates rise or the issuer's credit quality worsens
A higher-yielding bond usually signals higher risk, not a 'free' extra return
entries.bestFor: Investors comfortable assessing credit risk who want more income than government bonds, as part of a diversified fixed-income allocation.
entries.eligibility: 18 years old and above with a CDP/brokerage account for SGX-listed retail bonds; some corporate bonds are restricted to accredited or institutional investors.

entries.name: Fixed Deposits
entries.summary: Locking a lump sum with a bank for a fixed period in exchange for a guaranteed interest rate, with your principal protected by Singapore's deposit insurance scheme up to the coverage limit.
entries.analogy: Like agreeing not to touch a chunk of your savings for a set number of months, and the bank pays you a small thank-you in return.
entries.minAmount: Varies — see official page (banks each set their own minimum placement amount)
pros: Principal is protected under the SDIC Deposit Insurance Scheme, up to the coverage limit per bank
Interest rate is guaranteed and known upfront for the full tenor
Very simple to open, often instantly via internet banking
Wide range of tenors, from 1 month to a few years, to match your needs
cons: Breaking the deposit early usually forfeits most or all of the promised interest
Returns don't always keep pace with inflation
Foreign-currency fixed deposits are not covered by SDIC insurance
No capital growth potential — purely a place to earn interest safely
entries.bestFor: Beginners parking a lump sum they won't need for a fixed period and want a guaranteed, simple return.
entries.eligibility: Available to anyone with a bank account at a participating bank; some promotional rates require new funds or a minimum tenor.

entries.name: Cash Management Accounts
entries.summary: Accounts offered by robo-advisors, banks and brokerages that invest your idle cash into low-risk money market or short-term bond funds, aiming for a better return than a savings account while staying easy to withdraw.
entries.analogy: Like parking your spare cash with a slightly more hardworking cousin of a savings account — a bit more return, a very small amount of extra risk.
pros: Typically no lock-in — withdraw within a few business days
Historically higher yield than a basic bank savings account
Low minimum investment, often S$1 or S$0 to start
Diversified across many short-term, high-quality debt instruments
cons: Not principal-guaranteed and not covered by SDIC deposit insurance, unlike a bank fixed deposit
Yield can fall as interest rates fall, unlike a fixed deposit's locked-in rate
The underlying fund could in theory face liquidity stress in extreme market conditions
Marketed as 'cash-like' but is technically a market investment, not a deposit
entries.bestFor: Beginners wanting a flexible, higher-yielding home for emergency funds or cash waiting to be invested.
entries.eligibility: 18 years old and above; available through robo-advisor, bank or brokerage platforms offering these accounts.

entries.name: CPF Voluntary Cash Top-Ups (RSTU)
entries.summary: Voluntarily adding cash into your own or a loved one's CPF Special/Retirement Account under the Retirement Sum Topping-Up Scheme, to grow retirement savings faster and potentially reduce your income tax.
entries.analogy: Like putting extra cash into a locked, government-backed retirement piggy bank that also gives you a tax rebate.
pros: CPF interest rates are generally higher than most bank savings or fixed deposit rates
Cash top-ups to yourself or eligible family members can qualify for income tax relief
The Government matches top-ups for lower-income seniors under the Matched Retirement Savings Scheme
Boosts future CPF LIFE monthly payouts in retirement
cons: Money is locked in CPF until the eligible withdrawal age — not accessible for emergencies
Top-ups are irreversible once made
Tax relief has an annual cap, so large top-ups don't get unlimited tax benefit
Less flexible than other investments — no capital growth, purely interest-based
entries.bestFor: Singapore Citizens/PRs confident they won't need the cash before retirement, who want a low-risk way to boost retirement income and reduce this year's tax bill.
entries.eligibility: Singapore Citizens and Permanent Residents with a CPF account; topping up a loved one requires their CPF account details.

entries.name: Endowment Plans
entries.summary: A savings insurance plan where you pay premiums over a fixed term in exchange for a lump-sum payout at maturity, combining a small amount of life insurance with a mostly guaranteed-plus-bonus savings component.
entries.analogy: Like a forced-savings jar with a lock timer and a bit of insurance glued on — you can't easily open it early without losing money.
pros: Combines disciplined saving with a small life insurance payout
Guaranteed portion gives more certainty than pure market investing
Encourages long-term saving through fixed premium commitments
Participating plans may pay bonuses on top of the guaranteed amount
cons: Cashing out early usually returns less than what you paid in (surrender loss)
Non-guaranteed bonuses are not certain and can end up lower than illustrated
Returns are typically lower than investing directly in stocks or ETFs over the long run
Locks up your money for years with limited flexibility
Insurance and distribution charges reduce your net return versus a pure investment
entries.bestFor: Risk-averse savers who want a guaranteed savings discipline for a specific goal, such as a child's education, and don't mind lower expected returns.
entries.eligibility: Available to most adults through licensed insurers or financial advisers; medical underwriting may apply.

entries.name: Investment-Linked Policies (ILPs)
entries.summary: A policy that bundles life insurance with an investment in sub-funds of your choice — your premiums buy fund units, some of which are sold each month to pay for insurance and other charges.
entries.analogy: Like a two-in-one gadget that's both an umbrella and an investment account — convenient, but neither job is done as cheaply as buying them separately.
pros: Combines life insurance coverage with market-linked investment growth potential
You can usually switch between sub-funds as your goals or risk appetite change
A single monthly premium covers both protection and investing
Useful for long-term goals where you specifically want insurance and investing bundled together
cons: No guaranteed cash value — you can lose a significant part or all of your investment
Insurance and fund charges reduce the amount actually invested, especially in early years
Buying insurance and investments separately is usually cheaper overall
Complex to compare across insurers due to layered charges
MAS classifies ILPs as complex products requiring extra care before purchase
entries.bestFor: Investors with a long horizon who specifically want insurance and investment bundled in one policy and understand the extra layer of charges.
entries.eligibility: Available to most adults through licensed insurers or financial advisers; involves a needs analysis and sometimes a Customer Knowledge Assessment.

entries.summary: Buying physical gold/silver, a bank gold or silver savings account, or a gold-backed ETF as a store of value that tends to hold up when stocks and currencies wobble. It pays no income — you only gain if the price rises.
entries.analogy: Like keeping a chunk of your wealth in a form that doesn't rely on any company or government promise — the flip side is it doesn't pay you rent or dividends while you hold it.
pros: Historically holds value during high inflation or market stress
Gold/silver savings accounts and ETFs let you invest without storing physical metal
Easy to buy and sell through major banks or on the exchange
Diversifies a portfolio that is otherwise all stocks and bonds
cons: Pays no dividend or interest — your only return is price appreciation
Prices can still be volatile in the short term
Unallocated savings accounts are not covered by SDIC deposit insurance
Converting to physical bars or coins incurs an extra fee, plus storage and security to think about

entries.summary: Buying digital tokens like Bitcoin or Ethereum through an exchange licensed by MAS under the Payment Services Act. Prices are extremely volatile and, unlike bank deposits, your holdings are not protected if the exchange fails.
entries.analogy: Like betting on a highly speculative, fast-moving asset with no safety net — using a licensed platform reduces some risks, but it does not protect your capital.
pros: Using a MAS-licensed exchange reduces, but does not eliminate, counterparty and fraud risk
24/7 trading and easy access via app
Potential for large gains during bull markets
Wide range of tokens and growing mainstream acceptance

Extreme price volatility; you can lose your entire investment
Unlicensed platforms actively target Singapore users — always check the MAS register first
No dividends or interest; returns depend purely on price speculation

entries.name: Options & CFDs (Advanced, High Risk)
entries.summary: Leveraged instruments that let you speculate on price moves using a fraction of the position's value, magnifying both gains and losses. These are classified as Specified Investment Products and require passing a knowledge assessment before you can trade them.
entries.analogy: Like using a loan to bet on a race — a small win becomes a bigger win, but a small loss can become a bigger loss than you put in.
pros: Leverage means you can gain a large exposure with a smaller upfront outlay
Can be used to hedge existing stock positions against price falls
Wide range of markets accessible — indices, forex, commodities, single stocks
Flexible — can potentially profit from both rising and falling prices
cons: You can lose more than your original deposit, especially with CFDs
Most retail accounts trading CFDs lose money, according to industry-wide risk disclosures
Requires passing a Customer Knowledge Assessment (CKA) or Customer Account Review (CAR) first
Margin calls can force you to top up funds quickly or have your position closed at a loss
Not suitable for beginners — no dividend or income component, pure speculation

entries.name: Physical Property vs REITs
entries.summary: Buying physical residential or commercial property directly gives you full control and mortgage leverage, but ties up large capital and incurs taxes and upkeep — compared with buying REITs, which gives diversified property exposure from as little as one lot with far more liquidity.
entries.analogy: Owning physical property is like buying a whole apartment block; owning a REIT is like buying a few shares in a company that owns many apartment blocks for you.
pros: Direct property lets you use mortgage leverage to amplify potential gains
Full control over the asset — renovate, rent out, or occupy as you wish
A tangible asset that can also serve as your own home
Rental income plus potential capital appreciation over the long term
cons: Very high capital outlay, plus Buyer's Stamp Duty and possibly Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty
Illiquid — selling a property can take months and involves large transaction costs
Concentrated risk in a single asset and location
REITs offer similar property exposure with far smaller capital, instant liquidity and professional management, but you give up direct control
entries.bestFor: Those with substantial capital and a long horizon who want direct control; beginners wanting property exposure with small capital should consider S-REITs instead.
entries.eligibility: Property purchase is subject to eligibility rules (citizenship, existing property count) and financing approval. REITs are open to any investor with a CDP/brokerage account.

entries.name: Do-It-Yourself Investing
entries.summary: Open a brokerage account yourself and buy individual stocks, ETFs or bonds directly, deciding exactly what to hold and when to trade. You do your own research and pay the broker's trading costs directly.
entries.analogy: Like cooking your own meal instead of ordering a set menu — more control over every ingredient, but you do the work.
pros: Full control over exactly which stocks, ETFs or bonds you own
Usually the lowest-cost way to invest since you're not paying for advice or portfolio management
CDP-linked accounts put shares in your own name — dividends and voting rights come straight to you
Widest range of products across SGX, US, HK and other markets

No automatic diversification — concentration risk if you buy too few names
Choosing between CDP-linked and custodian accounts can be confusing at first

entries.name: Supplementary Retirement Scheme (SRS)
entries.summary: A voluntary account that gives you dollar-for-dollar income tax relief on what you contribute (up to a yearly cap), while the funds can be invested in stocks, ETFs, unit trusts, SSBs and more.
entries.analogy: Like a tax-advantaged wallet — money you put in shields part of your income from tax, and it can still be invested to grow.
pros: Dollar-for-dollar income tax relief on contributions up to the annual cap (differs for Citizens/PRs vs foreigners — see IRAS/MOF for the exact figure)
SRS funds can be invested across a wide range of products, not just left as cash
Withdrawals at the statutory retirement age get a meaningful tax concession compared to withdrawing early (see IRAS for exact terms)
One SRS account can be opened with any of the three local banks
cons: Early withdrawal before the statutory retirement age is taxed in full and attracts an extra penalty (see IRAS for exact terms)
You can only hold one SRS account at a time
Uninvested SRS cash earns a very low interest rate
Contribution cap and withdrawal rules can change — always check the official page
entries.bestFor: Higher-income earners who want to lower their tax bill this year while building a separate, investable retirement pot.
entries.eligibility: 18 years or older with taxable income in Singapore; the annual contribution cap and tax relief are set by IRAS/MOF.

entries.name: CPF Investment Scheme — Ordinary Account (CPFIS-OA)
entries.summary: Invest part of your CPF Ordinary Account savings — above a set amount that must stay untouched — in CPFIS-approved stocks, ETFs, unit trusts, bonds and more, aiming to beat the OA interest rate.
entries.analogy: Like taking a portion of a low-interest savings jar and putting it to work in approved investments, while keeping a safety cushion behind.
pros: Potential to earn more than the OA's guaranteed interest rate over the long run
Wide range of CPFIS-approved products — stocks, ETFs, unit trusts, bonds, gold
No extra cash needed — uses CPF savings you already have
Can be combined with cash/SRS investing for a fuller picture in the Compare tool
cons: You must set aside a minimum amount in your OA before investing the rest (see official CPF page for the exact figure)
Investment returns must beat the OA interest rate after fees to be worthwhile — many CPFIS investors underperform
Caps apply on how much of your investible savings can go into stocks vs gold (see official CPF page for exact limits)
Requires completing the CPFIS Self-Awareness Questionnaire and comes with sales charges/brokerage on top
entries.bestFor: CPF members confident they can beat the OA interest rate after fees, over a long investment horizon.
entries.eligibility: 18 years or older, not an undischarged bankrupt, OA savings above the required set-aside amount, and completion of the CPFIS Self-Awareness Questionnaire.

entries.name: CPF Investment Scheme — Special Account (CPFIS-SA)

entries.analogy: Like the more cautious sibling of CPFIS-OA — a smaller, safer menu of investments for money meant for retirement.
pros: Access to a curated, lower-risk list of CPFIS-SA-approved investments
Potential to earn more than the SA's guaranteed interest rate over the long run
No extra cash needed — uses CPF savings you already have
Can sit alongside CPFIS-OA and cash/SRS investing for a full retirement plan
cons: Only available to CPF members below age 55 — the Special Account closes at 55 and folds into the Retirement Account (see official CPF page)
You must set aside a minimum amount in your SA before investing the rest (see official CPF page for the exact figure)
SA's own interest rate is relatively high, so the bar to beat it after fees is higher than for OA
Narrower product list than CPFIS-OA — mainly unit trusts and select bonds
entries.bestFor: CPF members under 55 with SA savings well above the set-aside amount, who are confident of beating the SA interest rate after fees.
entries.eligibility: Below age 55, not an undischarged bankrupt, SA savings above the required set-aside amount, and completion of the CPFIS Self-Awareness Questionnaire.

pros: Combines insurance protection with an investment component in one policy
Endowments offer a defined savings target for goals like education or retirement
Premiums are often structured to build a savings discipline automatically
Some ILPs let you switch between sub-funds as your risk appetite changes
cons: Bundling insurance and investment usually costs more than buying each separately
Early surrender often means getting back less than what you paid in
ILP investment returns are not guaranteed despite the insurance wrapper
Fee structures (insurance charges, fund charges, distribution costs) can be hard to compare across policies
entries.bestFor: People who specifically want insurance protection bundled with a savings/investment target, understanding the extra cost.
entries.eligibility: Varies by insurer and policy; medical underwriting may apply for the insurance component.

entries.name: Licensed Financial Adviser
entries.summary: Work with a MAS-licensed financial adviser or representative who assesses your full financial picture and recommends specific products, for a fee and/or commission.
entries.analogy: Like hiring a personal trainer instead of following a workout app — more tailored guidance, at a higher cost.
pros: Personalised advice that considers your full financial situation, not just investments
Can help with complex needs — estate planning, insurance gaps, retirement projections
A human to talk to during volatile markets, which can prevent panic decisions
Some advisers charge a flat fee instead of commission, aligning incentives more closely
cons: Commission-based advisers may be incentivised to recommend higher-fee products
Advisory and platform fees add up over time compared to DIY investing
Quality varies widely between advisers — always check their licence and track record
You still need to understand what you're buying — advice doesn't replace your own diligence
entries.bestFor: People with complex finances, or who want a professional relationship to guide major financial decisions.
entries.eligibility: No special eligibility; check that the adviser or representative is licensed with MAS before engaging.

steps.detail: Provide income, expenses, existing policies and goals so the advice is properly tailored.

pros: Much wider fund shelf than a single bank, across many fund houses
Often lower or zero sales charges compared to buying the same fund via a bank branch
Can consolidate cash, SRS and sometimes CPF investments in one account
Research tools and fund fact sheets to compare options side by side
cons: Platform fees still apply, even where sales charges are waived
Overwhelming choice for a first-time investor without a plan
Customer support is typically online/phone-based rather than in-branch
Some products require extra risk acknowledgements before you can buy them
entries.bestFor: Investors who want to shop across fund houses and often pay less than going through a bank branch.
entries.eligibility: 18 years or older; account opening via Singpass MyInfo or manual verification.

entries.name: Employee Share Schemes
entries.summary: Some employers let staff buy company shares at a discount (ESPP) or grant shares/options as part of compensation (ESOP/RSU). Shares are usually held via a plan administrator chosen by your employer.
entries.analogy: Like getting a staff discount, but the 'purchase' is shares in the company you work for.
pros: Discounted purchase price (for ESPPs) creates an immediate paper gain if the share price holds
Aligns your financial interest with your employer's performance
Often deducted automatically from payroll, building a saving habit
No brokerage account needed to participate — the employer's plan handles this
cons: Concentration risk — your income and a chunk of your investments depend on the same company
Vesting schedules and blackout periods restrict when you can sell
Tax treatment of gains/options can be complex — check IRAS guidance
Illiquid until shares vest and any company-imposed holding period ends
entries.bestFor: Employees at companies offering share plans, as a supplement to — not a replacement for — a diversified portfolio.
entries.eligibility: Set by your employer; typically requires a minimum tenure before you can participate or before shares vest.

pros: Shares are registered in your own name at CDP — dividends and voting rights (e.g. AGM invites) come directly to you
Long-established players regulated by MAS, with decades of track record
Access to IPOs, rights issues and corporate actions handled directly via CDP
Full range of order types and, for many, access to remisier/full-service support
cons: Commissions for cash accounts are typically higher than app-based custodian brokers
Opening a CDP account is an extra step compared to custodian brokers
Platforms can feel dated compared to newer mobile-first apps
Custody/settlement fees may apply if you trade infrequently
entries.bestFor: Investors who want SGX shares registered in their own name and don't mind a slightly higher cost for that.
entries.eligibility: 18 years or older with a CDP Securities account; a Singapore bank account is generally required for CDP's direct crediting service.

entries.analogy: Like a currency exchange counter for a currency that can swing wildly in value overnight — the counter being licensed doesn't make the currency itself safe.

24/7 market access and near-instant transfers between exchanges/wallets
Wide range of digital assets available compared to traditional brokers

cons: Extreme price volatility — cryptocurrency values can fall sharply and rapidly

Not covered by SDIC deposit insurance or the same investor protections as securities
Common target for scams — always transact only through the exchange's own licensed app or site
entries.bestFor: Only experienced investors who understand and accept the risk of losing their entire investment; not a starting point for beginners.
entries.eligibility: 18 years or older; identity verification required. Always confirm current licensing status on the MAS Financial Institutions Directory before transacting, as licences and entities can change.
